narration: [serious] By 1944, every Marine rifle squad was built around one weapon, carried three times over.
[short pause] It was designed in 1917 for another war: to be fired from the hip while walking toward the enemy.
Twenty rounds in the magazine. At full speed, about two seconds of fire.
It weighed about twenty pounds, and its barrel could not be changed when it overheated.
Yet in Korea, soldiers called it indispensable, and could not imagine fighting without it.
[pause] This is how a walking gun became the weapon an entire squad was built around.
[measured] When America went to war in 1917, its troops in France were issued French automatic weapons, like the Chauchat.
The French had a doctrine for them. Attacking infantry carried automatic rifles forward and fired as they walked,
keeping the enemy's heads down until the line reached his trench. [short pause] It was called walking fire.
John Browning, the country's best-known gun designer, built a better weapon for that job in 1917. His son Val, seen here in 1918, would later demonstrate it against the Germans himself.
It was gas-operated. A little gas from each shot was tapped off the barrel. It drove back a piston, and the piston was connected to the slide that worked the action.
Moving back, the slide compressed a spring. The spring then drove it forward again to load the next round.
The result was the M1918: a full-power rifle cartridge, a twenty-round box magazine, and about sixteen pounds of weight. Light enough for one man to carry in an assault.
A lever on the left chose semi-automatic, automatic, or safe.

Production started in 1918, but General Pershing held the new rifle back, so the Germans would not capture one too early. [short pause] The 79th Division finally took it into action in September 1918. It was used widely in the Meuse-Argonne offensive, the largest American offensive of the war.
The Marines wanted it too. Men of the 6th Marines talked Army troops into a trade: their Chauchats for BARs.
[short pause] On October 9, 1918, an order came down. Every Browning in Marine hands was to be turned in.
By the armistice in November, fifty-two thousand had been built. [short pause] It came too late to change the war. But the Army had found a weapon it would keep for the next forty years.
[thoughtful] Between the wars, Army training films still taught it as a rifle. On automatic, standing, it emptied its magazine in one long burst.

The numbers explain why that mattered. At about five hundred and fifty rounds a minute, twenty rounds last a little over two seconds. [short pause] The Army's own manual put the most effective rate at only a hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty rounds a minute.
As a new war came closer, the Army faced an awkward fact: it had no portable light machine gun for its rifle squads.
So on June 30, 1938, it turned the BAR into one. The new M1918A2 got a bipod near the muzzle, and a mechanism in the stock to slow its rate of fire.
It lost its semi-automatic setting, and now fired only on full automatic, at a fast or a slow rate. [short pause] With its sling, it weighed about twenty pounds.
And it got a new job. When the Army entered the Second World War, the BAR was the only automatic weapon in its twelve-man rifle squad.
[measured] On paper, the squad had a leader, an assistant leader, seven riflemen,
and one three-man automatic rifle team, built around the BAR:
a gunner, an assistant who carried more magazines and could take over, and an ammunition bearer. [short pause] Here, a BAR team of the 325th Regiment fires on advancing Germans in December 1944.
In the Army's plan, the riflemen were the attack.
The BAR supported them as a base of fire, pinning the enemy down while the riflemen moved forward.
In combat, units bent the rules. Some ran one-man BAR teams, with every rifleman carrying spare magazines.
Many Army divisions put two BAR teams in each squad, so one could keep firing while the other reloaded.
They were copying an idea that had come out of the Pacific, [short pause] where the Marine Corps had gone much further and rebuilt its whole squad around the gun.
[curious] In early 1944, the Marines reorganized their rifle squads. A squad of thirteen was split into three fire teams of four, and every one of those teams was built around a BAR.

[firm] Compare the two. The Army squad had one BAR supporting eleven other men. [short pause] The Marine squad had three. Each team had a corporal in command, a rifleman, an assistant automatic rifleman, and the automatic rifleman himself. The riflemen were there to protect and feed the gun.

On paper, a Marine rifle company now carried twenty-seven BARs, and a regiment two hundred and forty-three. Across a division, the count rose from about five hundred in 1943 to more than eight hundred and sixty by 1945.

In the jungle, BAR men often walked near the head or the tail of a patrol, where a sudden burst could break an ambush on a narrow trail. This Marine on Cape Gloucester, in January 1944, carries his ready to fire.
Many Marines threw the bipod away to save weight.
In many ways, the BAR went back to what Browning had first designed:
an automatic rifle carried by one man, fired from the shoulder or the hip, moving with the riflemen around it.
On Okinawa in 1945, the 6th Marine Division fought through ridges like these with fire teams built around the BAR.
[short pause] For the Marines, the BAR was no longer just a support weapon. It was the center of the team.
[serious] That center came at a price, and the BAR man paid it.

With its sling, the gun alone weighed about twenty pounds, more than twice an M1 rifle. Each loaded magazine added almost a pound and a half. [short pause] In Korea, a gunner's belt held twelve of them, and many carried three or four more in their pockets.
And it was not a simple gun. A 1925 training film walks soldiers through its stoppages and its small, breakable parts.
The barrel was screwed into the receiver. It could not be swapped out when it grew hot in a long fight.
Real light machine guns, like the British Bren, could change barrels in the field.
[measured] It also needed constant care. The rate reducer in the stock was a delicate spring-and-weight system. One ordnance sergeant called it a Rube Goldberg device.
In the humid Pacific, its gas cylinder, never made of stainless steel, could rust solid unless it was cleaned every day.
Kept clean, it was rugged and reliable.
But the next war would test it harder.
[somber] In Korea, the BAR went to war a third time. Many were old weapons rebuilt in Japan, and in the hard winter of 1950, some of them failed.

One Army battalion, the 2nd of the 38th Infantry, lost faith in its BARs after the fighting near Kunu-ri. [short pause] When the failures were checked, almost every gun that had quit was a reconditioned one, cleaned but left with its old springs.
New guns, straight from the factory, had almost no trouble at all.
The man who recorded this was the military historian S. L. A. Marshall.

[firm] In 1951 he interviewed infantrymen across Eighth Army for an Army research office. His conclusion was blunt. The BAR, even more than the machine gun, was the fire base the whole fight was built around. One BAR man, he wrote, could quiet a sniper-infested area better than five or six riflemen.
Wherever the rifle line began to bend, he found, commanders sent the BARs to hold it.
Riflemen were willing to carry extra ammunition for it.
His verdict: the BAR in Korea merits a clean bill.
And he passed on what the troops asked for: double the number of BARs.

[measured] The numbers show how long America leaned on it. About a hundred and two thousand were built for the First World War. [short pause] More than a hundred and eighty-eight thousand new ones came in the Second, on top of older guns rebuilt. During Korea, the Royal typewriter company built sixty-one thousand more.
A young soldier who fought there, David Hackworth, later called it the best weapon of the Korean War.

[reflective] By the 1950s, the BAR was more than thirty years old. The Army began replacing it with an automatic version of the M14 rifle, and from 1957 with the belt-fed M60 machine gun. [short pause] Its story runs in a straight line: a walking gun in 1918, a squad machine gun in 1938, the heart of the Marine fire team in 1944.
So was it a good light machine gun? No.
Its magazine was too small, and its barrel was fixed.
But that was never really its job.
It was an automatic rifle that one man could carry anywhere a rifleman could go.
[pause] In 2010, the Marine Corps chose a new weapon for the automatic riflemen in its fire teams: the M27, a light, magazine-fed automatic rifle, picked to replace a belt-fed machine gun.
The idea John Browning built in 1917, one man carrying the fire of a machine gun, had come back.
[reflective] It had been built to walk. In the end, a whole squad walked around it.
